messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 20
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Interior Designer
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 37

At twenty, she is newly married and works as an interior designer, a job she once imagined would mark the beginning of an adult life she had chosen for herself. She spends her days thinking about light, texture, and proportion—how a room can be made to feel calm, open, safe. When she talks about work, she still brightens for a moment, describing color palettes and fabric samples spread across a table. But the idea of safety has become complicated for her, because the person who hurt her most is the man she married.

She met him when she was still very young, and in the beginning she remembers him as attentive, protective, and intensely interested in her. He praised her sketches, told her she had an eye for beauty, and said he wanted to build a life with her. Not long after they married, his attention became something heavier. He wanted to know where she was, who she was with, why she took too long to answer a message. At first she explains it away as stress, jealousy, or love expressed badly. She tells herself that all couples argue, that marriage requires patience, that she can keep the peace if she says the right thing in the right tone.

The first time he hits her, it happens during an argument in their home. She remembers not the whole conversation but a series of sharp details: the way his jaw tightens, the smell of dinner cooling in the kitchen, the sudden disbelief that flashes through her just before his hand strikes her face. For a second, she cannot make sense of what has happened. Then her ears ring, her cheek burns, and she feels a wave of shame before she feels anger. He apologizes afterward, crying and holding her, saying he was out of control, saying it will never happen again. She wants desperately to believe him. She believes marriage means staying, trying, forgiving.

But the violence repeats. Sometimes it is a shove into a wall, a grip around her wrist that leaves marks, a hand at her throat just long enough to make her freeze. Sometimes it follows accusations that make no sense to her. Sometimes it comes after nothing she can identify at all. She begins to live in anticipation. She watches the set of his shoulders when he enters a room. She listens to the weight of his footsteps. She studies his silence like it is a language she must master to survive. She learns to keep her own voice soft and her body small. Even when he is not angry, her muscles stay tense, as if they no longer trust stillness.

At work, she starts changing in ways her colleagues do not fully understand. She has always been careful with detail, but now she startles when someone comes up behind her at her drafting table. If a client raises their voice, even in ordinary frustration, her heart races and her mind goes blank. She sometimes loses track of conversations in meetings because she is pulled back into memories she does not want—his hand on her arm, the sound of something breaking, the trapped feeling in her chest. When she visits clients’ homes, she catches herself scanning exits, noticing doors, windows, narrow hallways. She tells herself it is part of being observant, part of her training, but she knows it is more than that.

Nights are the worst. She dreads going to sleep because she often wakes abruptly, soaked in sweat, unsure for a few seconds where she is. In dreams, there is pressure, shouting, the sense that she cannot get away. Sometimes her husband is asleep beside her and she lies rigid, afraid to move, listening to his breathing. Other times, if he shifts suddenly or reaches for her in bed, she flinches before she can stop herself. She hates that reflex. She says it makes her feel disloyal, even though another part of her feels furious that her body has learned this fear so well.

She has become more withdrawn from friends and family. It is hard to explain why she cancels plans, why she rarely answers calls, why crowded places exhaust her. She worries people will see something in her face and ask questions she is not ready to answer. She also worries they will not ask, and that this means what is happening to her is somehow ordinary. At times she feels detached from herself, as if she is watching her life through glass. She stands in beautiful rooms she has helped create—spaces designed for comfort and warmth—and feels almost nothing.

What troubles her most in the present is how constantly she remains on guard. A slammed door sends a jolt through her body. A man arguing on the street makes her change direction. If she notices a bruise-colored pattern in fabric or paint, she is suddenly back in the room where he hurt her. She tells herself she should be stronger, should be able to move on, especially because from the outside she still looks composed: a young wife, a creative professional, someone building a future. But underneath that appearance, her days are organized around avoiding reminders, managing fear, and questioning her own memory. She still longs for spaces that feel the way she designs them to feel—settled, breathable, safe—and she cannot yet find a way to live inside one.
